title:
The Sentinel of the Secret Chambers: The Biographical, Mystical, and Geopolitical Legacy of Rabbi Meir Yehuda Getz

Rabbi Meir Yehuda Getz (1924–1995) served as Rabbi of the Western Wall and the Holy Sites for nearly three decades, from 1967 until his death. His tenure coincided with one of the most dramatic periods in modern Jewish history—the return of Jewish sovereignty to the Old City of Jerusalem following the Six-Day War. Getz became a central figure not only in the religious administration of Judaism's holiest site but also in clandestine archaeological endeavors and mystical activities that reflected his profound messianic worldview. This article examines Getz's biography, his kabbalistic orientation, his involvement in the search for the Temple vessels and the Ark of the Covenant, and his influence on the religious-political discourse surrounding the Temple Mount.

Getz was born in 1924 in the Old City of Jerusalem to a family of Hasidic lineage. He studied in various yeshivot in Jerusalem and was ordained as a rabbi. After the 1948 War of Independence, when the Jewish Quarter fell to Jordanian forces, Getz was among those expelled from the Old City. For nineteen years he lived in western Jerusalem, serving in educational and rabbinical roles. The liberation of the Old City in June 1967 was for him a personal and national redemption. He was among the first to return to the Western Wall plaza immediately after its capture, and within a short time was appointed Rabbi of the Western Wall, a position specially created for him in recognition of his deep connection to the site and his religious stature.

In his capacity as Rabbi of the Western Wall, Getz oversaw prayer arrangements, maintained cleanliness and order at the site, and served as a spiritual address for countless visitors—Jews and non-Jews alike—who came to the Western Wall. However, his activities extended far beyond routine administration. Getz saw himself as responsible not only for the Western Wall's present but also for uncovering its past and preparing for its future. He believed with perfect faith that the Temple vessels, including the Ark of the Covenant and the menorah, were hidden in subterranean chambers beneath the Temple Mount, and that discovering them would hasten the redemption and the building of the Third Temple.

During the 1970s and 1980s, Getz conducted—with support from certain government elements and without official permits—a series of underground excavations near and beneath the Western Wall. He worked primarily in the Western Wall tunnels, a network of subterranean passages running along the Western Wall's length beneath the buildings of the Muslim Quarter. Getz believed he had identified the precise location where the Temple vessels were concealed, based on his study of rabbinical sources, mystical traditions, and kabbalistic texts. In 1981, he and a group of yeshiva students broke through a wall in the tunnels and entered a large underground cistern located beneath the Temple Mount itself—known as "Warren's Gate Cistern"—seeking the hidden vessels.

This activity led to a serious incident: when Muslim worshippers at the Al-Aqsa Mosque discovered the Jewish presence beneath the Mount, violent riots erupted. The Israeli government, fearing a regional conflagration, ordered the immediate sealing of the opening, and Getz was compelled to halt the excavations. The affair remained partially classified for years, but became a legend in religious-nationalist circles and a source of ongoing controversy. Getz never abandoned his conviction that the vessels were there, and until his final days continued to study maps, sources, and testimonies in an attempt to locate them.

Getz's worldview was deeply rooted in Kabbalah and Hasidism. He saw the Western Wall not merely as a historical remnant but as a living entity possessing spiritual vitality and metaphysical significance. According to his perception, the Shekhinah (Divine Presence) had never departed from the Western Wall, and the site served as the primary conduit between the earthly and heavenly realms. He would spend long hours in solitary prayer at the Wall, particularly in the tunnels and hidden chambers, and was reputed to experience mystical revelations and dreams providing him with instructions and hints regarding the Temple vessels' location.

In his teachings and conversations, Getz frequently emphasized the obligation to prepare practically for building the Third Temple. He was not content with passive messianic longing but believed in active human initiative to hasten the redemption. This outlook placed him at the forefront of the movement for Temple preparation and connected him with organizations and activists working toward Jewish access to the Temple Mount and establishing Jewish sovereignty there.

Getz's influence on the religious and political discourse in Israel was considerable. His persona combined halakhic authority, mystical inspiration, and nationalist activism. He was admired by the religious-Zionist public and sectors of the Haredi community, and maintained connections with political figures who supported his activities. Simultaneously, he was a controversial figure: secularists and moderates viewed him as a dangerous messianic extremist whose actions could ignite regional conflict; the Muslim world saw him as a symbol of Jewish intentions to seize the Temple Mount and destroy the mosques.

Beyond the archaeological and political aspects, Getz was also an educator and spiritual guide. Thousands passed through the Western Wall plaza during his tenure, and many testified to his personal warmth, his willingness to listen and offer blessings, and his ability to create an atmosphere of holiness and elevation. For many visitors, an encounter with Rabbi Getz was a formative spiritual experience.

Rabbi Meir Yehuda Getz died in 1995 and was buried on the Mount of Olives. His legacy remains contested: to his supporters, he was a visionary who understood the times and worked with devotion and self-sacrifice to reveal the Temple's sanctity and prepare for redemption; to his critics, he was a symbol of the dangers inherent in messianic activism and the politicization of religion. In any case, there is no doubt that Getz was one of the most fascinating and influential figures in Jerusalem's religious landscape during the second half of the twentieth century, and that his activities continue to resonate in contemporary discussions about the Temple Mount, messianism, and the relationship between religion and state in Israel.

Getz adopted the ascetic regimen characteristic of the yeshiva's inner circle. He slept a mere three hours nightly, dedicating the pre-dawn hours to midnight tikkunim (mystical devotions) and immersive study of the Zohar and the writings of the Arizal (Rabbi Isaac Luria).[1] His daily schedule included prayers at sunrise in the chamber closest to the Holy of Holies, followed by administrative duties at the Western Wall plaza, teaching responsibilities at Yeshivat Beit El, and nocturnal mystical study.[1] He maintained strict personal disciplines, including periodic fasting and immersion in the mikveh (ritual bath) before dawn.[1]

His mystical worldview profoundly influenced his custodianship of the Western Wall precinct. He believed that certain subterranean spaces beneath the Temple Mount retained latent sanctity and prophetic potential, and he devoted considerable effort to exploring and documenting the labyrinthine network of tunnels, cisterns, and ancient passageways that honeycomb the area.[1] His intimate knowledge of this underground topography would soon thrust him into the center of a volatile religious and geopolitical controversy.

The Warren's Gate Incident: Archaeology, Eschatology, and Political Crisis

The most dramatic episode in Getz's tenure occurred in 1981 (תשמ"א), when excavations he was overseeing in the Western Wall tunnels led to the breaching of Warren's Gate (Sha'ar Warren), an ancient Herodian portal sealed for centuries, which opens directly onto the Temple Mount plaza.[3, 4, 5] According to Getz's own account and that of corroborating witnesses, workers under his supervision broke through into a large, concealed chamber beneath the Mount, which he believed might lead to, or actually contain, the Ark of the Covenant and other sacred Temple vessels hidden before the Babylonian destruction.[3, 4, 5]

News of the breach spread rapidly, igniting fierce opposition from the Muslim Waqf (Islamic religious trust), which administered the surface of the Temple Mount.[3, 4] Fearing that the excavation represented a prelude to Jewish reclamation of the Mount or the rebuilding of the Temple, the Waqf orchestrated riots and threatened widespread violence.[4, 5] Within hours, Waqf laborers poured tons of concrete into the chamber from above, sealing it and any treasures it may have contained.[3, 5] The Israeli government, wary of inflaming regional tensions and potential international fallout, ordered the immediate cessation of all work and the resealing of Warren's Gate from the Jewish side.[4, 5]

Getz was devastated. He publicly lamented that he had been "mere meters" from the Ark, and that political cowardice had squandered a once-in-millennia opportunity to recover the lost vessels and perhaps accelerate the messianic redemption.[3, 5] In interviews, he expressed profound frustration with the secular authorities' prioritization of diplomatic considerations over spiritual destiny.[5] Nevertheless, he complied with the government's directive, and the incident was suppressed in the public discourse for several years.[4]

The affair profoundly illustrated the collision of mystical aspiration, archaeological ambition, religious sovereignty, and realpolitik in Jerusalem. It also cemented Getz's reputation—among supporters as a heroic guardian of Jewish sacred memory, and among critics as a religious zealot willing to risk regional conflagration for eschatological ends.[4, 5]

Defender of Sacred Space: Public Service and Personal Piety

Beyond the subterranean drama, Getz's decades of public service were marked by meticulous attention to the sanctity and accessibility of the Western Wall plaza. He supervised the daily liturgical life of the site, maintained its ritual purity, mediated disputes among diverse Jewish communities seeking to pray there, and ensured respect for halakhic standards in a space visited by millions annually.[1] He was known for his personal warmth, greeting visitors from all backgrounds, offering blessings, and providing pastoral care to soldiers, mourners, and pilgrims.[1]

His dual identity—as a salaried state official and as a mystical adept—was a source of both strength and tension. He reported formally to the Ministry of Religious Affairs, yet his spiritual loyalty was to his teachers in the esoteric tradition and to what he perceived as divine imperatives that transcended bureaucratic authority.[1] This occasionally placed him at odds with governmental directives, particularly when those directives conflicted with his understanding of sacred duty.

Despite the burdens of public office, Getz never abandoned his rigorous mystical practice. He continued to rise before dawn, pray with intense concentration (kavvanah) in proximity to the Holy of Holies, study kabbalistic texts, and guide students in the hidden dimensions of Torah.[1] His life embodied the kabbalistic ideal of unifying the revealed and concealed, the outer administration of communal sacred space and the inner cultivation of divine consciousness.

Legacy and Memory: The Guardian of Jerusalem's Walls

Rabbi Meir Yehuda Getz passed away on the 23rd of Tishrei, 5755 (September 28, 1995), and was buried on the Mount of Olives alongside his sons.[1] His funeral was attended by thousands, including senior rabbis, government officials, and ordinary Jerusalemites whose lives he had touched.[1]

In the years since his passing, Getz has been memorialized in multiple registers. Within the kabbalistic community, he is revered as a link in the chain of the masters of Yeshivat Beit El, a guardian of the Rashash's mystical tradition.[1] Among Religious Zionist circles, he is celebrated as a symbol of the synthesis between devotion to the land, military valor, and halakhic commitment.[1] In popular memory, the Warren's Gate episode has achieved near-legendary status, inspiring books, documentaries, and conspiracy theories about what lies beneath the Temple Mount.[3, 4, 5]

Critically, Getz's life invites reflection on the tensions inherent in the modern Jewish return to sovereignty over sacred space. His biography encapsulates the challenges of administering sites charged with eschatological meaning within the framework of a secular democratic state navigating a volatile geopolitical environment. His willingness to risk political crisis in pursuit of sacred relics reflects a worldview in which ultimate religious values supersede temporal prudence—a stance that continues to animate debates within Israeli society.

Conclusion

Rabbi Meir Yehuda Getz stands as a singular figure in the landscape of twentieth-century Jewish religious leadership. His trajectory from a Tunisian rabbinic family through wartime survival, Zionist activism, pioneering settlement, military service, mystical devotion, and custodianship of Judaism's holiest site reflects the multifaceted nature of modern Jewish experience. His attempts to penetrate the secrets beneath the Temple Mount—whether quixotic or prophetic—underscore the enduring power of sacred geography and eschatological hope in shaping Jewish action.

Ultimately, Getz's legacy rests not only in his institutional accomplishments or his dramatic exploits, but in his embodiment of a life wholly dedicated to the service of the sacred. In an era of fragmentation and specialization, he modeled an integrated religious personality: soldier and mystic, administrator and ascetic, public servant and private devotee. As the sentinel of Jerusalem's secret chambers, he guarded not only physical gates and tunnels, but the permeable boundary between history and redemption, between the revealed city and the city of divine promise.

His personal conduct was defined by ascetic rigor. He adopted a highly structured routine, retiring for sleep only between the evening prayer (Maariv) and midnight.[1] At midnight, he descended into the subterranean chambers of the Western Wall to recite Tikkun Chatzot (the Midnight Liturgy) directly opposite the estimated location of the Holy of Holies, studying kabbalistic texts there until the sunrise prayer (Vatikin).[1] After completing his administrative duties as Rabbi of the Western Wall, he dedicated his afternoons to teaching at Yeshivat Beit El.[1]

Despite his personal asceticism, Getz advocated a philosophy of domestic harmony and peace. He maintained strict entrance requirements for Yeshivat Beit El, making a student's admission contingent upon the maintenance of peace within their home (Shalom Bayit).[1] In his private life, he modeled this behavior by showing profound respect for his wife, establishing a custom of presenting her with a gift or piece of jewelry at the start of every Hebrew month (Rosh Chodesh).[1]

Getz left behind a significant corpus of written works spanning kabbalistic theory, biblical commentary, and historical documentation.[1, 2] His primary kabbalistic work, Reshpey Esh ("Flashes of Fire"), is a commentary on the esoteric intentions (kavanot) of the Rashash, structured around the classical systems of Rabbi Isaac Luria (the Ari) and Rabbi Chaim Vital.[1] Written in dense, classical rabbinic style, Reshpey Esh remains a core text for advanced students at Yeshivat Beit El, studied under the guidance of his student, Rabbi Yisrael Avichai.[1] His other works include Gitzei Torah ("Sparks of the Torah"), a volume of homiletical and mystical commentaries on the Pentateuch, and Kuntres HaKotel ("The Western Wall Treatise"), which outlines the halakhic history of the site.[2] He also composed specialized essays on domestic harmony (Ma'amar Shalom Bayit), the sanctity of the Land of Israel (Ma'amar Eretz Yisrael), and the spiritual significance of Jerusalem (Ma'amar Yerushalayim), alongside two liturgical poems written during and after the Six-Day War.[2]

The Archeology of Redemption: The Gate of the Priests and the Warren's Gate Crisis

The most historically complex chapter of Getz's tenure began in the early 1970s with the systematic excavation of the Western Wall Tunnels, a project he initiated and directed.[3] In 1971 (תשל"א), workers uncovered a massive sealed gate along the Western Wall.[3] Getz identified this structure as the "Gate of the Priests," believing it to be the ancient portal through which ritually impure priests departed the Temple Mount complex.[3] His historical calculations suggested that this gateway lay on a direct trajectory to the subterranean chambers where King Josiah had hidden the Ark of the Covenant before the destruction of the First Temple.[3] According to the Mishnah, the Ark had been safely hidden "in winding underground chambers" (במטמוניות עקלקלות).[3] Eager to pursue this discovery, he drafted a letter to the Lubavitcher Rebbe, Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson, in New York.[3] The Rebbe responded with a firm warning, stating that the sanctity of the Temple Mount must be strictly guarded and that any subterranean excavations beneath the holy site should be suspended.[3] Getz accepted this ruling and paused the project.[3]

However, the situation changed dramatically in August 1981 (תשמ"א). During ongoing preservation and clearance works, excavators accidentally breached a wall adjacent to "Warren's Gate"—a subterranean portal named after the nineteenth-century British archaeologist Charles Warren.[3, 4] This gateway was a key entrance to the Temple Mount during the late Second Temple period, famously documented by Josephus.[5] Behind the breached wall lay a massive cavern, measuring approximately 28.5×5.5 meters with a height of 10.70 meters, which had functioned as a water cistern (designated as Cistern 30 in Warren's survey).[5] In ancient times, this chamber served as a subterranean passage from which people climbed to the Mount via stairs.[5]

Getz believed this cavern was a key to the Temple's ancient foundations and a direct pathway to the hidden Ark.[3] He immediately organized operations to pump out the water and mud that filled the chamber.[3] Because of the sensitive nature of the site, the work was kept quiet, but news of the excavation gradually leaked to political figures and eventually appeared in the national media.[3]

The public revelation of the excavation triggered an immediate geopolitical crisis, drawing protests from Islamic authorities (the Waqf) and sparking concerns of widespread civil unrest.[3] Tensions escalated when Waqf workers breached the cistern from an entrance on top of the Temple Mount.[3] Getz rushed to the site, where he found himself facing an angry crowd.[3] Armed with his personal sidearm, he held his ground until yeshiva students and security forces arrived to secure the area.[3] To prevent further escalation, the Israeli government intervened.[3] Workers from the Waqf built a concrete wall approximately 3 to 4 meters thick across the middle of the cavern.[3] Concurrently, Israeli authorities ordered the entrance sealed from the Western Wall side, permanently closing the passage and ending Getz's efforts to locate the Ark.[3, 4]

The Halakhic Debate and the Structural Sanctity of the Getz Synagogue

The closure of Warren's Gate did not end spiritual activity at the site. Instead, it led to a significant halakhic discussion regarding the boundaries of the Temple Mount and the status of subterranean spaces.[5] The central question was whether entering the gateway of Warren's Gate violated the strict prohibition against ritually impure individuals (teme'im) entering the Temple Mount complex.[5]

Guardian of the Walls and Repositories of the Secret: The Work, Thought, and Torah Teaching of Rabbi Meir Yehuda Getz

The text surveys the extensive life work of Rabbi Meir Yehuda Getz, a multi-dimensional figure who bridged the worlds of halakha, the mystical, and practical Zionism in the State of Israel. The survey follows his growth in Tunisia, through his aliyah to the Land and his military service, to his extended tenure as Rabbi of the Western Wall and head of the kabbalists' yeshiva "Beit El." Special emphasis is placed on his unique kabbalistic teaching that advocated combining Torah with work and service in the IDF, alongside documentation of the historical struggle to uncover the Western Wall tunnels and locate the Ark of the Covenant. The purpose of the source is to present the legacy of a spiritual leader who saw in the redemption of Jerusalem and in devotion to the collective of Israel the goal of his work, while combining personal asceticism with deep public involvement.

Guardian of the Walls and Repositories of the Secret: The Work, Thought, and Torah Teaching of Rabbi Meir Yehuda Getz

The figure of Rabbi Meir Yehuda Getz represents an exceptional fusion of halakhic authority, public leadership, mystical deepening, and Zionist-pioneering activism in the State of Israel of the twentieth century.[1, 2, 3] Rabbi Getz, who united in his personality the worlds of the revealed and the hidden, served for approximately twenty-eight years as Rabbi of the Western Wall and the Holy Places, and simultaneously led the historic kabbalists' yeshiva "Beit El" in the Old City of Jerusalem.[1, 4, 5] This report analyzes in depth his life history, the unique foundations of his kabbalistic thought, his public and scholarly enterprises, and the historical struggles he conducted concerning the uncovering of Jerusalem's secrets.[1, 2, 3]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Beginning of the Path in Tunisia: The Growth of a Torah Scholar and Jurist in the Shadow of War

Rabbi Meir Yehuda Getz was born on the fifteenth of Av 5684 (August 15, 1924) in the town of Menzel Bou Zelfa in Tunisia, to a family that combined agricultural work with extensive rabbinic lineage.[1, 2] His mother, Simcha-Mas'uda, was a descendant of Rabbi Chaim ben Attar, author of the commentary "Or ha-Chaim" ha-Kadosh on the Torah, and his father was Rabbi Tsemach Getz, a scion of a well-known rabbinic family.[1, 4] In his childhood the family moved to the city of Tunis, where he was educated at the Talmud Torah "Or ha-Torah" and displayed exceptional talent that led him to successfully demand the integration of French language studies alongside religious studies.[1, 4] He studied with the great Torah scholars of Tunisia, foremost among them Rabbi Yehoshua Pitusi, who later made aliyah and served as rabbi of the city of Safed.[1, 4] In his youth Rabbi Getz was distinguished by his inclination for language acquisition, and developed deep mastery of ten different languages, including Hebrew, Arabic, Ladino, German, Esperanto, Yiddish, Latin, Romanian, Italian, and Turkish.[1]

The period of World War II brought with it severe upheavals; in 1944 Rabbi Getz was taken for forced labor by Nazi German forces in the city of Bizerte.[1] Even under the harsh conditions of enslavement he maintained his identity and looked after the Jewish needs of his fellow camp inmates, and even wrote a Megillat Esther in secret under the noses of the German guards.[1] On the fifteenth of Shevat 5703, at the height of a British bombardment of the area, he exploited the commotion and fled from the camp wearing a soldier's uniform he had received, and made his way on foot to his home a distance of approximately 60 kilometers.[1] Following the miracle of his salvation, he vowed to celebrate the day of the fifteenth of Shevat every year.[4]

At age 19 he married Esther-Silvet of the Gaz family, and the two established their home in the town of Nabel.[1, 4] Parallel to his work for a livelihood, he completed legal studies by correspondence at the prestigious Sorbonne University in Paris.[1, 4] In the year 5706 (1946), at only 22 years of age, he was ordained as a rabbi, and the following year was qualified as a lawyer and notary.[1, 4] He was appointed rabbi of the town Souk el-Arba (Jendouba) in northwestern Tunisia, and served there simultaneously as cantor, mohel, ritual slaughterer, and officiant at weddings.[1, 4] In this role he brought children close to Torah study and worked energetically within the framework of the Zionist movement, while influencing members of his community to make aliyah to the Land of Israel and encouraging the youth to train in self-defense and weapons bearing.[1] After the establishment of the state, he responded to the call of the Jewish Agency and moved to Grenoble in France, where for about a year he ran an institution of Youth Aliyah and imparted to his students – among them, later, Rabbi Yitzhak Chaim Peretz – Torah, Zionism, and love of the Land.[1]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Galilee Period and the Move to Jerusalem: Crisis and Bereavement as a Spiritual Springboard

At the end of the year 5709 (1949) Rabbi Getz made aliyah to Israel with his wife and four children.[1] Initially they were housed at the Halisa transit camp in Haifa, where the rabbi worked as a simple laborer in initiated works of the Jewish National Fund, and subsequently, by virtue of his mastery of languages, was appointed as a clerk at the Ministry of Labor.[1] After a few months he was called to serve as rabbi, cantor, mohel, and ritual slaughterer in the moshav "Ha-Har ha-Adom" (whose name was later changed to Kerem Ben Zimra) in the Upper Galilee.[1, 6] In this moshav he directed spiritual life, founded the elementary agricultural school "Benayahu" and served as its first principal.[1, 4] In 1952, even though he was exempt from mandatory service as a father of four children, he enlisted voluntarily in the IDF, completed a mortar commanders' course and an officers' course, and reached the rank of lieutenant colonel as commander of a 120mm mortar battery and as security coordinator of the Merom HaGalil area.[1, 6] His diverse activity earned him in 1956 special recognition from the President of the State as one of the "choice persons of the year."[1]

The event that fundamentally changed the course of his life occurred during the Six-Day War in 1967.[1, 6] His second son, Avner-Shimon, who fought as a paratrooper in the 55th Brigade, fell in the historic battle at Aب al-Sahira (the Muslim cemetery adjacent to the Lions' Gate) during the battles for the liberation of Jerusalem.[1, 6] Despite the enormous pain, the rabbi received the news with great faith and told his family members that woe unto him that this had happened to him, but fortunate is he that he merited that his son fell for the liberation of Jerusalem.[1, 6] Following the son's death, the rabbi and the rebbetzin decided to move their residence to Jerusalem in order to live near their son's grave at Mount Herzl.[1, 6] In 1971 they were among the first families to settle in the liberated Jewish Quarter, in a house that had served in the nineteenth century as a Sephardic Talmud Torah.[1, 6]

Rabbi Getz left behind an extensive family that took an active part in shaping Israeli society and public service.[1] The family legacy combines broad security, municipal, and legal activity.[1]

The Family of Rabbi Getz and His Distinguished Descendants

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

His Torah and Kabbalistic Teaching: The Unique Path of Study and the Three Paths

The Torah teaching of Rabbi Getz was characterized by exceptional breadth of horizons and direct drawing from a wide variety of halakhic and kabbalistic traditions.[3] Even before he began to deepen in the teachings of the Ari and the Rashash (Rabbi Shalom Sharabi), he dedicated many years to systematic study of foundational books from all corners of the world of Jewish thought.[3] He studied in depth the books of "Ma'or va-Shemesh" on the Torah, the commentary "Ha-Sulam" of Rabbi Yehuda Ashlag on the Sefer ha-Zohar, all the writings of the Ba'al Shem Tov, the books of the Hasidism of Komarno, the books of the Gra, the books of "Leshem Shevo ve-Achlamah" of the kabbalist Rabbi Shlomo Elyashiv, and also the books of Chabad Hasidism and especially the teaching of the Admor ha-Zaken, the Ba'al ha-Tanya.[3]

Rabbi Getz experienced a significant study crisis when he was learning in chavruta with Rabbi Margaliot in the north of the country.[3] The two felt a deep difficulty in understanding the words of the Ari and their practical application, to the point of a feeling of a dead end.[3] Rabbi Getz decided to continue and deepen again, relying on a saying of Chazal that establishes that a Torah scholar who does not see a sign of blessing in his study for five years will no longer see.[3] He testified that precisely from the insistence on passing the threshold of five years, new gates of understanding opened before him, and he began to see blessing
his profound depth in the study of the esoteric.[3]

Rabbi Getz's intellectual conduct was characterized by absolute integrity and uncompromising striving toward truth.[3] He was accustomed to summarize in writing every lesson and sugya that he taught.[3] However, when he discovered during his studies that the conclusions he had reached in his writings did not correspond in their precise spirit to the spirit of the holy books he had received from his teachers, he did not hesitate and completely shelved all his old writings and began to write his teaching anew out of humility and self-abnegation.[3] His central kabbalistic work, Reshafei Esh, he wrote out of a sense of deep longing and a quest for pure truth.[3] The rabbi noted in his introduction that the merit of the fallen soldiers of the Six-Day War, among whom was his son Avner Shimon, stood by him and illuminated his path to arrive at an understanding of the secrets of the Torah.[3] Alongside this work, the rabbi wrote Gitsei Torah—a unique kabbalistic commentary on the weekly Torah portions, Kuntres HaKotel, halakhic and philosophical essays on topics concerning Jerusalem, the Land of Israel, and shalom bayit (domestic harmony), and even composed two poems about Jerusalem reflecting the experience of transition from destruction to redemption.[1]

In his introduction to his book Reshafei Esh, Rabbi Getz presents a systematic and philosophically profound distinction among three central paths in the esoteric wisdom.[3] This distinction serves as a key to understanding his conception of the role of the kabbalist in the modern generation.[3]

Comparison among the three paths of Kabbalah in Rabbi Getz's teaching

In addition to his deepening in esoteric Torah, Rabbi Getz displayed impressive openness to the sciences and external wisdoms.[3] He dedicated a significant portion of his free time to the study of fields such as astronomy, medicine, philosophy, and natural science, and held the view that understanding the general sciences is a necessary tool for understanding the depth of the Torah.[3] He was accustomed to bring as support the well-known dictum of the Vilna Gaon that to the extent that a person lacks knowledge of worldly wisdoms, he will lack one hundred measures in the wisdom of Torah.[3] This openness and his charismatic personality left a powerful impression even on non-Jews; in one instance he conducted debates and philosophical discourse with a Christian priest and French intellectual, who declared to him at the conclusion of their meetings that if he continued to converse with him—ultimately he himself would convert to Judaism.[3]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Restoration of the Beit El Yeshiva of Kabbalists and His Spiritual Practices

The yeshiva of kabbalists "Beit El" was founded in the year 5493 (1733) in the Jewish Quarter of Jerusalem by Rabbi Gedaliah Hayon, and over the generations became a magnet for kabbalists from all over the world.[5, 7] After the destruction of the Quarter in the War of Independence, the yeshiva continued to operate partially in the Yegi'a Kapayim neighborhood under the leadership of Rabbi Ovadia Hedaya.[5] In 1973, Rabbi Getz initiated the restoration of the historic and abandoned building in the Jewish Quarter, and reestablished the branch of the yeshiva in the Old City, at whose head he stood until his last day.[1, 5] Rabbi Getz invested all his energy in building the yeshiva, both on the spiritual side and the physical side, and a mere three days before his passing he merited participating in the dedication of the magnificent and restored building in its original location.[1, 4] After his death, his distinguished disciple, Rabbi Yisrael Avihai, was appointed to continue his path at the head of the yeshiva.[1, 5]

Rabbi Getz fashioned for the yeshiva a unique and revolutionary admission protocol that reflected his conception that the study of Kabbalah requires full partnership in building the nation and in practical life.[3] This protocol was based on two uncompromising conditions for accepting students[3]:

Active service in the IDF: Rabbi Getz saw in the State of Israel the beginning of the sprouting of our redemption, and believed that one who is not a partner in the defense of the people and the land cannot be a true partner in the mystical processes of redemption.[3] Beyond this, he held that the experience of military service instills in a person self-sacrifice, devotion, and abnegation of individuality for the sake of the collective—traits that constitute a necessary spiritual foundation for entering the gates of esoteric Torah without personal and egoistic orientations.[3]

Economic independence ("benefiting from the labor of one's hands"): The rabbi required of the yeshiva students to engage in gainful employment that enables them to support their families with dignity.[3] According to his approach, a person who supports himself is a free person who is not dependent on the charity of others or on institutional stipends, and thereby his intellectual and spiritual freedom is preserved to express his views and the truths of the Torah without fear.[3]

Rabbi Getz's daily schedule was characterized by meticulous asceticism, austerity, and iron self-discipline.[2, 4] He sufficed with very few hours of sleep, sleeping only during the sparse hours between the evening prayer and midnight.[4] Every night, precisely at midnight, he would rise for the recitation of "Tikkun Hatzot" facing the site of the Holy of Holies in the Western Wall tunnels, where he would weep over the exile of the Shekhinah and study Torah and Kabbalah continuously in the morning watch until the prayer at sunrise.[2, 4] After a demanding workday at the Western Wall plaza, he would turn to teach at Beit El Yeshiva until the evening prayer.[4] In order to withstand the enormous physical and spiritual burden of this daily schedule, he was careful to maintain high physical fitness and performed daily calisthenics in his private room.[2]

Despite his personal asceticism, Rabbi Getz utterly rejected practices of tension or sadness at home.[4] He emphasized to his family members and students that domestic peace and harmony take precedence over all, and conditioned the acceptance of students to the yeshiva on the existence of "shalom bayit" on the part of the candidate.[4] He treated his wife with remarkable respect and intense love; the two shared a plate and utensils at every meal, and the rabbi was careful to give her a piece of jewelry or special gift on every Rosh Hodesh as a token of appreciation for her support of his endeavors.[2, 4]

His Service as Rabbi of the Western Wall and the Writing of the "Western Wall Diary"

In the year 5729 (1969), Rabbi Getz was appointed by the then Minister of Religious Affairs, Dr. Zerach Warhaftig, to serve as Rabbi of the Western Wall, and subsequently his appointment was expanded to Rabbi of the Holy Sites in the Land of Israel.[1, 4] In this role he served as the central address for every halakhic, public, and administrative matter at the Western Wall plaza for approximately twenty-eight years.[1] He became known by the epithet "the social worker of the Kotel" due to his warm and loving attitude toward every person; he dedicated long hours to assisting those in need, distributed money and loans to the needy many of which were never repaid, and even saw to the welfare and livelihood of beggars and Arab guards who worked in the area.[2] The rabbi acted out of a deep moral conception according to which every person is created in the image of God, this despite having lost his son in battle against Arab forces.[2]

Throughout all his years of service, Rabbi Getz maintained in a Sisyphean and meticulous manner the "Western Wall Diary."[1, 2] The diary, spanning 12 thick volumes totaling approximately 3,600 pages in his handwriting, constitutes a historical and personal document of unique value.[1, 2] The writing of the diary began a week after his appointment and continued uninterruptedly until three days before his passing.[2]

In the volumes of the diary, the rabbi was accustomed to record precise hours and dates, often every two hours.[2] He documented an extraordinary combination of topics[1, 2]:

Daily and operational events at the plaza, such as sewage explosions, power outages, coordination of prayers, security incidents, and garbage removal.

Meetings with state leaders, prime ministers, presidents, and ambassadors from Israel and the world who visited the Western Wall.

Detailed description of the progress of archaeological excavations in the Western Wall tunnels, which he closely accompanied and guided.

Complex public and halakhic struggles to preserve the unifying character of the Wall against interest groups, including archaeologists, various religious streams, Women of the Wall, and politicians.

The diary reveals Rabbi Getz's tremendous efforts to prevent disputes and to preserve the Wall as a place of national consensus that accepts every Jew as he is.[2] Today, the "Beit HaRav Getz" foundation, established by his family members to preserve his legacy, is leading a major project to publish the volumes of the diary to the public

## The Uncovering of the Western Wall Tunnels and the Historical Drama of Warren's Gate (1981)

Rabbi Getz was among the initiators and leaders of the uncovering of the Western Wall Tunnels, which he viewed as a kind of "time tunnel" connecting the people of Israel directly to the days of glory of Jerusalem in the Second Temple period.[2, 8] He believed with perfect faith that the discovery of the Ark of the Covenant and the Temple vessels, which according to the Mishnah and tradition were hidden in "intricate caches" beneath the Temple Mount, would bring about the nullification of the exile and the coming of the Messiah.[9, 10]

Despite his enthusiasm, the great scholars of the generation dissuaded him more than once from direct involvement in these searches.[10] In 1976 he sought to begin focused excavations to locate the Ark, but Rabbi Zvi Yehuda Kook (HaRaZYaH) restrained him, saying: "Do not dig."[10] A detailed inquiry he sent to the Lubavitcher Rebbe in New York was answered with a decisive written response in the Rebbe's own handwriting, which determined that the plan to dig tunnels beneath the Temple must be completely cancelled, even in the remotest doubt (*safek-safeika*) of impinging upon the sanctity of the place.[9] The Rebbe explained that the people of Israel were not spiritually prepared for this revelation, and expressed grave concern for the life of Rabbi Getz himself.[10] Rabbi Getz accepted the Rebbe's opinion and shelved the plans for several years.[9]

### The Discovery and the Secret Excavation

The turning point occurred on 20 Tammuz 5741 (22 July 1981).[10] During routine clearing work in the tunnels, an ancient stone wall was breached, exposing an arch that formed part of an ancient gate from the Second Temple period (known as "Warren's Gate") and a massive subterranean hall behind it.[10] Rabbi Getz was urgently summoned to the site by the work supervisor.[2, 10] Upon seeing the hall flooded with water and mud, the Rabbi was seized with tremendous excitement; according to his topographical calculations, the gate—which he called "the Priests' Gate"—led in a straight line to the hiding place of the Ark of the Covenant beneath the Holy of Holies.[9, 10] In his diary he described how he sat prostrate and powerless for a long hour as scalding tears streamed from his eyes, until he gathered courage and entered the space with enormous awe in order to recite *Tikkun Ḥatzot* (the Midnight Lament).[2, 10]

Out of a sense of historical mission, Rabbi Getz decided to continue excavating and clearing the hall "at any cost," writing in his diary the dramatic words: "I have come to kill and to be killed."[10] He obtained the secret consent of the Chief Rabbis, Rabbi Shlomo Goren and Rabbi Ovadia Yosef, to establish a synagogue in the exposed space.[10] On the advice of Rafi Eitan, who then served as the Prime Minister's adviser on terrorism, it was decided to conceal the excavation from Prime Minister Menachem Begin to spare him political pressures that would compel him to halt the initiative.[10]

The evacuation of the putrid water and mud from the massive cistern (cistern no. 30 of the explorer Charles Warren) encountered many technical difficulties.[9, 10] Since regular fire brigade services could not be used due to fear of leaking the secret through Arab firefighters, members of Kibbutz Sde Eliyahu and volunteers from the Ministry of Religious Affairs were recruited for the work.[10] These individuals evacuated the mud manually, bucket by bucket and wheelbarrow by wheelbarrow, under Rabbi Getz's close and daily supervision.[10]

### The Leak and the Violent Confrontation with the Waqf

After approximately a month of secret excavation, the breaching of the wall became known to archaeologists who opposed the initiative, and Jerusalem Mayor Teddy Kollek leaked news of the excavation to the press.[10] The publication aroused enormous international uproar and threats of riots from Israeli Arabs and Arab states.[9, 10] The government ordered the cessation of work, but the drama reached its climax at noon on Wednesday, 4 Elul 5741 (3 September 1981).[10] Agents of the Muslim Waqf exploited the quiet in the tunnels, lowered themselves from the Temple Mount plaza through an opening in the cistern into the hall, and smashed the wooden barriers that the Jews had erected with the aim of sealing the gate with concrete from within.[9, 10]

The police who were on site fled, and Rabbi Getz remained alone facing dozens of Arab rioters who hurled stones, blocks, and iron bars at him.[9, 10] The Rabbi drew his personal pistol, stood in the entrance, and threatened them not to advance.[9] When his wife, Rebbetzin Esther, arrived at the site and urged him to flee to save his life, the Rabbi replied to her with sangfroid: "Your son Avner was killed here, and I too, your husband, am prepared to fall here."[10] Subsequently, students from the yeshiva "Ateret Cohanim" arrived and secured the site at his side against the rioters.[9, 10]

In the end, the police arrested specifically the Jewish demonstrators.[10] By direct order of Prime Minister Menachem Begin and Interior Minister Yosef Burg, and under heavy pressure from United States Ambassador Samuel Lewis, the gate was completely closed and sealed by the pouring of a thick concrete wall approximately four meters thick on both sides of the Western Wall.[9, 10] The blocking of the gate caused Rabbi Getz the deepest despondency and a severe spiritual crisis.[10] He compared the feeling to the destruction of the Temple and wrote in his diary with great pain:

"Every blow of the Arabs inside the tunnel, apparently sealing the interior of the wall with thick concrete... pierces like a sword in my wounded heart."[10]

His daughter Lilly testified that he required considerable time to recover from the shattering of his great dream to bring the Temple vessels and the Ark of the Covenant to light and to hasten the redemption.[10]

## His Passing, Commemoration, and Legacy for Generations

On 23 Elul 5755 (18 September 1995), only three days after he had the privilege of realizing his great aspiration and dedicating the restored permanent building of the kabbalists' yeshiva "Beit El," Rabbi Getz suffered a heart attack and passed away.[1, 4] He was buried in a mass funeral at the cemetery on the Mount of Olives, near the holy sites where he had labored and guarded for a jubilee of years.[1]

Rabbi Getz's work and legacy are commemorated today in diverse ways, expressing the appreciation of Israeli society for his unique character:

**Ma'alot HaRav Meir Yehuda Getz (Steps of Rabbi Meir Yehuda Getz):** The stairway leading from the Western Wall plaza toward the Jewish Quarter and Jaffa Gate was named in his honor.[1]

**The Synagogue in the Name of Rabbi Getz:** The magnificent synagogue situated within the Western Wall Tunnels, opposite the site of the Holy of Holies, which was established at his initiative, was named after him following his death.[1]

**Beit HaRav Getz and the Commemoration Association:** His historic home in the Jewish Quarter today serves as a center for hospitality, tours, and study for groups and travelers.[1] In 2015, the "Beit HaRav Getz" association was established to connect Israeli society to his figure, and in 2025 his personal and professional archive was deposited for preservation and research.[1]

**Figure of the Year of HEMDAT (Center for Religious State Education):** In the year 5778 (2018), Rabbi Getz was declared "Figure of the Year" of religious state education, and his life story and teachings were studied in kindergartens and schools throughout the country.[1]

**Literature and Documentary Film:** His life story has been commemorated in the extensive biographical book *Rav HaKotel* (*Rabbi of the Western Wall*) by Simcha Raz (extending over 502 pages) and in the documentary film *Ish HaEmunah* (*Man of Faith*) produced by Adir Zik and Yael Alon.[1, 11, 12]

Rabbi Meir Yehuda Getz remains in the national memory as a symbol of complete spiritual leadership that lived its life from within a constant and fruitful tension between the esoteric and the exoteric, between theoretical reflection and pioneering action, and between the private pain of bereavement and absolute self-sacrifice for the sake of the people of Israel, its Torah, and its Land.[1, 2, 3]
